title: Citizen Scientists Uncover the Twisty Evolutionary Path of Harvestmen Fatherhood
summary: In the world of arachnids, harvestmen—those spindly, spider-like creatures often called daddy longlegs—are exceptional fathers. Now, thanks to an army of citizen scientists, we know their path to fatherhood has been anything but straightforward. An international team led by the University of São Paulo reconstructed the evolutionary history of parental care in the superfamily Gonyleptoidea and found that guarding behavior appeared, vanished, and reappeared multiple times. The study, published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, leveraged iNaturalist, a platform where anyone can upload georeferenced wildlife observations. From 1936 to 2025, scientific literature documented egg-guarding in only 80 harvestman species. In just two days of searching iNaturalist, researchers added 62 new records, effectively doubling the dataset. This rapid accumulation of data allowed them to trace how maternal and paternal care evolved. Maternal care consistently arose from ancestors with no care, mirroring patterns in insects. Paternal care, however, followed two distinct routes: it either evolved directly from no-care species or from species where females already guarded eggs. This latter path suggests a form of sexual selection called 'enhanced fecundity,' where females preferentially mate with males already caring for eggs—essentially, good dads get more offspring. Harvestmen are a model group for studying paternal care because they represent more than half of all independently evolved cases among arthropods, despite comprising only 0.6% of arthropod diversity. Lead author Glauco Machado emphasized that iNaturalist's true power is accessibility: 'I would never be able to do this by visiting museums around the world. It would be very expensive, very time consuming.' Yet expert taxonomists remain crucial; distinguishing true parental care from similar behaviors like mate guarding requires specialized knowledge. The study not only illuminates the complex evolution of fatherhood but also showcases how citizen science can democratize and accelerate biological research, particularly for scientists in the Global South.
why_it_matters: By revealing how fatherhood evolved repeatedly in harvestmen, the study provides insight into the evolution of family life and demonstrates that citizen science can rapidly advance knowledge, offering a model for low-cost global research.

background_read: Parental care—behavior by parents to improve survival of offspring—has evolved many times across animals, including in fish, frogs, and insects; paternal care is particularly rare.
The superfamily Gonyleptoidea is a diverse group of harvestmen, mostly in South America, where many species guard eggs on vegetation or on their own bodies.
iNaturalist, launched in 2008, is a joint project of the California Academy of Sciences and the National Geographic Society; its data are used in hundreds of scientific papers each year.

Glauco Machado, a researcher at the University of São Paulo (Brazil's leading university), studies arachnid behavior and has long used iNaturalist to track harvestmen observations across South America.
The Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society is a prestigious publication dating back to 1856, focusing on evolutionary biology and taxonomy.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Harvestmen (daddy longlegs) are exceptional fathers, but their evolutionary path has been twisty
└─ Citizen scientists via iNaturalist double known egg-guarding species
KEY FINDING: Paternal care appeared, vanished, and reappeared multiple times in Gonyleptoidea
├─ Maternal care always arose from no-care ancestors
└─ Paternal care evolved either from no-care or from maternal-care ancestors
MECHANISM: Enhanced fecundity—females prefer males already caring for eggs, boosting offspring
└─ This sexual selection route suggests 'good dads' get more mates
DATA SOURCE: 80 literature records + 62 iNaturalist records in two days
└─ iNaturalist's georeferenced photos replace costly museum visits
IMPORTANCE OF HARVESTMEN: >50% of independent arthropod paternal care cases, only 0.6% of diversity
└─ Glauco Machado (lead author) highlights iNaturalist accessibility for Global South scientists
CAVEAT: Expert taxonomists still needed to distinguish true parental care from mate guarding
BROADER IMPACT: Citizen science accelerates evolutionary biology and democratizes research

perspectives.description: Enthusiasts of citizen science applaud how an army of amateurs can speed up scientific discovery and democratize research, giving people everywhere a stake in understanding biodiversity.

Some professional taxonomists caution that distinguishing true parental care from similar behaviors like mate guarding requires expertise, and misidentifications could skew results if not carefully verified.

The pattern of paternal care evolving from maternal care suggests that once females provide care, it creates opportunities for males to take over, a transition seen in some fish and insects, hinting at a general evolutionary rule.

Integrating AI species identification with iNaturalist could further accelerate research, but ensuring data quality and training more taxonomists remain essential for harnessing the full power of citizen science in conservation.
